text: Today's hearing on child care since the pandemic, macroeconomic impacts of public policy measures. I want to get right to the point. Federal child care funding is on the verge of a massive funding cliff. This cliff has the potential to cause more than three million children across this country

speaker: SPEAKER_00
text: to lose their care, and the impacts will ripple throughout our whole economy.

speaker: SPEAKER_01
text: But here's the kicker. We here in Congress have the power to stop this. And that's why we're having today's hearing, and that's why I am so happy that we have our witnesses here today: Glenn Hopkins, who runs a child care

speaker: SPEAKER_02
text: center; Sarah Hardy, co-founder and COO of an infant formula company; and Catherine Edwards, an economist and an expert on the labor market.

speaker: SPEAKER_02
text: They

speaker: SPEAKER_01

speaker: SPEAKER_03
text: workers, for parents and families, and for our whole economy.
Three

speaker: SPEAKER_00

a

speaker: SPEAKER_03

text: For decades, millions of working families have struggled to find care for their children, and if they are fortunate enough to find good care, millions struggle

text: to pay for it so they can go to work or to school. Access to high-quality child care is essential to our

speaker: SPEAKER_05
text: operate. And if businesses cut back because they can't find workers, then national productivity and economic growth
suffer.

speaker: SPEAKER_03

by

text: We have champions in the Senate willing to get this done. Last month, I joined Senator Kane, Smith, and 27 of our colleagues calling for $16 billion in emergency federal funding so child care providers can keep their doors open.

text: Just last week, the White House announced support for efforts to secure additional funding for child care, and I'm willing to reach across the aisle to work with any Republican who wants to help get this done. We've got one big opportunity before us this month.
